slides.text: More of the `slices` package. Searching with a rule, inserting and deleting values, removing duplicates, joining slices and making room.

`Index` and `Contains` look for one exact value. When the question is "the first item that fits a rule", `IndexFunc` and `ContainsFunc` take a function that answers true or false for each item.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
position of the first item where
    the rule is true

is the rule true for any item?

slides.text:
On a slice that is already sorted, `BinarySearch` is faster: it halves the range at each step. It answers with a position and a bool, and when the value is missing the position is where it would go.

`MaxFunc` and `MinFunc` pick the biggest or smallest item by your own rule.

exercises.title: Binary search
exercises.guide: Find a value in a sorted slice, or where it would go.

chunks.guide: A sorted slice. `BinarySearch` only works on sorted data. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.BinarySearch` returns the position and whether the value is there.
When the value is missing, the position is where it would go to keep the order.
A value bigger than all of them goes at the end: the position is the length.

exercises.title: Search with a rule
exercises.guide: Find the first item that fits a rule.

chunks.guide: A slice of numbers. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.IndexFunc` gives the position of the first item for which the function is true, or -1.

notes.text: True for the first item over 6.

chunks.guide: `slices.ContainsFunc` only says whether some item fits the rule.
When nothing fits, `IndexFunc` gives -1 like `Index`.

exercises.title: The first big number
exercises.guide: Print the position of the first number above 3, then whether there is one.

exercises.title: Biggest by a rule
exercises.guide: Find the longest and the shortest word.

chunks.guide: Three words of different lengths. The imports are already in the file.
`MaxFunc` and `MinFunc` take the same kind of rule as `SortFunc`. This one compares lengths.
`MaxFunc` returns the biggest item by the rule, and `MinFunc` the smallest.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.code:
ids := []int{5, 15, 25}
pos, found := slices.BinarySearch(ids, 15)
fmt.Println(pos, found)
pos, found = slices.BinarySearch(ids, 1)
fmt.Println(pos, found)
exercises.explanation: 15 is at index 1. 1 is missing, and it would go at the start, so the position is 0, never -1.

slides.text:
A slice cannot change its length in place, so `slices.Insert` and `slices.Delete` give back the slice you must use. Store it, or you keep the old one.

The snippet is real code with placeholder names.
slides.code:
s = slices.Insert(s, i, value)
s = slices.Delete(s, i, j)
s = slices.DeleteFunc(s, rule)

slides.text:
The range of `Delete` is like a cut: from `i` up to, but not including, `j`.

It works in the same array, shifting the items left, and it clears the tail that is left over. That tail is why the old slice looks different afterwards.

exercises.title: Insert values
exercises.guide: Put values into a slice at a chosen position.

chunks.guide: A slice with a gap in the middle. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.Insert` puts values in at an index and returns the new slice. Store the result.

notes.text: Insert may return a new slice.

chunks.guide: An index equal to the length adds at the end, like `append`.
Index 0 adds at the front.

exercises.title: Delete a range
exercises.guide: Remove items from a slice by position.

chunks.guide: Five letters. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.Delete(s, 1, 3)` removes the items from index 1 up to, but not including, index 3.

notes.text: Like a cut s[1:3], but removed.

chunks.guide: To remove one item, delete the range from its index to the next.

exercises.title: Use the result of Delete
exercises.guide: Call `Delete` and see what the old slice holds.

chunks.guide: Five numbers. The imports are already in the file.
`Delete` returns the shorter slice. Keep it in `t`.
The old `s` still has its length. `Delete` shifted the items left and cleared the freed tail to zero.

notes.text: The old tail now holds zeros.

chunks.guide: Only the returned slice has the right length.

exercises.title: Delete what fits a rule
exercises.guide: Remove every item that matches a rule.

chunks.guide: Six numbers. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.DeleteFunc` removes every item for which the function is true. Store the result.
Useful to drop empty strings from a list.

exercises.title: Add and remove
exercises.guide: Add 9 at index 1, then remove the first two items.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `Delete` shifts the rest left in the same array and clears the freed tail, so `s` ends with two zeros. Use the returned slice only.

slides.text: `slices.Compact` removes repeated values, but only runs of equal neighbours. On sorted data that means all the duplicates. `slices.Concat` and `slices.Repeat` build a new slice from others and leave the originals alone.

Two functions work on capacity, which you met in the slice capacity module. `slices.Clip` cuts the spare room off, like a three-index slice. `slices.Grow` asks for room up front, so a loop of appends does not reallocate.

The snippet is real code with placeholder names.

exercises.title: Remove duplicates
exercises.guide: Sort a slice, then drop its repeated values.

chunks.guide: Repeated values, mixed up. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.Compact` removes repeats that sit next to each other. Sort first so equal values are neighbours.
Store what `Compact` returns, as with `Delete`.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `Compact` only merges runs of equal neighbours. The two runs of 1 around the 2 each become one 1, and the 2 stays between them.

exercises.title: Join and repeat
exercises.guide: Build new slices from old ones.

chunks.guide: Two small slices. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.Concat` joins any number of slices into a new one.
`slices.Repeat` repeats a slice a number of times, in a new slice.
The originals did not change.

exercises.title: Clip the capacity
exercises.guide: Stop a piece of a slice from overwriting the rest.

chunks.guide: Five numbers. The imports are already in the file.
A piece shares the room of `s`, so `append` on it overwrites `s`.
Put the value back. `slices.Clip` cuts the capacity down to the length, like `s[:2:2]`.
There is no room left, so `append` makes a new array and `s` is safe.

exercises.title: Make room first
exercises.guide: Ask for room once, then append without reallocating.

chunks.guide: A short slice. The imports are already in the file.
`slices.Grow(s, 10)` makes sure 10 more items fit. The length stays the same, and the capacity is at least the length plus 10.
Appending up to that room never needs a new array, so the capacity does not change.

exercises.title: Join or repeat
exercises.guide: Join `a` and `b` into one new slice, then repeat `a` twice.
